planting.note: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; Susanville is a California-origin artichoke-type softneck bred from California Early stock and noted for reliable low-chill performance, adapting well to both warm and cold-winter climates alike.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Susanville is an artichoke-type softneck improved from California Early stock, valued for a wide climate range and dependable bulbing even where winters are too mild to satisfy hardneck garlic's chilling needs. Bulbs form in a layered, artichoke-like pattern with a good number of easy-to-peel cloves in white to lightly purple-streaked wrappers, carrying a robust flavor that mellows nicely when roasted or cooked. As a softneck it braids easily and cures into long-storing bulbs. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store for use through much of the year.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm — Artichoke variety descriptions
University of California Cooperative Extension — Garlic Production in California
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Garlic Variety Selection for Texas

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Sierra Blanca is an intermediate/short-day white hybrid onion widely recommended across Texas, New Mexico, and the Gulf South as one of the most reliable large sweet onions for home gardens.

directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this intermediate/short-day hybrid needs a southern winter's shorter daylight to bulb well. Sierra Blanca is an All-America Selections-winning white onion widely grown across the Southwest and Gulf South for its large, globe-shaped bulbs, crisp white flesh, and consistently mild, sweet flavor, making it a favorite for fresh eating as well as cooking. It bulbs reliably and stores somewhat better than the thinnest-skinned sweet onions, though it is still best used within a few months for peak quality. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and ease off watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Lincoln Leek (Dual-Purpose Baby and Full-Size Leek)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out once pencil-thick; Lincoln is a dual-purpose open-pollinated leek that can be pulled young as tender 'baby' finger leeks in about 50-60 days or left to size up to a full 16-20 inch stalk.

directions: Start Lincoln leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Lincoln is a flexible, open-pollinated leek that rewards impatient gardeners as well as patient ones — pull it young at 50-60 days for slender, tender 'baby' or finger leeks with a mild, delicate flavor, or let it grow on to a full-sized 16-20 inch stalk for a heartier harvest later in the season. Hill or trench soil around the growing stems to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion as the plants mature. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free, and harvest through fall and into winter in mild climates, since leeks tolerate cold far better than onions.

common_name: Tadorna Leek (Cold-Hardy Fall and Winter Leek)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or start in summer for a fall/winter main crop; Tadorna is a reliable open-pollinated leek noted for strong cold tolerance and good disease resistance, making it well suited to the Gulf South's cool-season leek window.

directions: Start Tadorna leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or start seed in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Tadorna is a dependable open-pollinated leek that produces long, thick, blue-green stalks with excellent cold tolerance, standing well in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough or bitter, and shows good resistance to common leek diseases. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, Tadorna can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window.
